# Postmortem

`customer_support.obj.postmortem.postmortem` · v1.0.0 · **draft** · scope **capability**

> The written account of what happened and what changes because of it. Two halves, and only one of them is the point: a timeline of the incident assembled from artefacts, and a list of actions each carrying a named person and a date. The timeline is the part everyone enjoys writing. The action list is the part that decides whether the exercise was worth the room.
The output of a postmortem is a changed system, not a document. A postmortem whose actions have no owner and no date is a diary entry — accurate, sincere, occasionally beautiful, and completely inert. It will be linked to approvingly for years while the same incident recurs, and its existence will make the recurrence harder to argue about, because the organisation can point at it and say the work was done.
The document is also a claim, and claims can be wrong. That is not a defect in the model; it is what makes the object worth having separately from the incident it describes.


**The discriminator.** The Incident is the event; the Postmortem is the claim about the event. The incident record can be right while the postmortem is wrong — and routinely is. The incident says impact ran 47 minutes because that is what the clock recorded; the postmortem says 12 because whoever wrote it started the timeline at declaration rather than at onset, which is the single most common error in the genre and the one that makes the detection gap disappear from the very document that exists to find it. When the two disagree, the incident record wins on facts and the postmortem wins on nothing.


Also called: `Post-Incident Review`, `PIR`, `RCA Document`, `Root Cause Analysis Report`, `Incident Review`, `After-Action Review`, `Learning Review`


### Questions this object answers

- Did anything actually change because of this incident, or did we only write about it?
- How long was it broken before we knew, and is that number moving across reviews?
- Which actions are overdue, who owns them, and what displaced them?
- Has this exact failure been reviewed before, and were those actions completed?
- Is the account of what happened trustworthy, or was it reconstructed from memory?
- Does this customer need a written RCA, and is the internal version safe to send?


### What it is NOT responsible for

- Not the incident itself — that is customer_support.obj.core.incident, which owns the clock, the blast radius, the severity and the communication stream while impact is live.
- Not the defect — that is customer_support.obj.core.issue, which outlives the incident and is closed by a fix rather than by a review.
- Not the causal finding — that is customer_support.obj.core.root_cause, which is a structured object other capabilities can read. The postmortem REFERENCES root causes and must not be the only place they are recorded, or the finding is trapped in prose.
- Not the engineering work — that is customer_support.obj.core.bug_report. An action item that never became a tracked engineering artefact has not left this document.
- Not incident communication during the event — that is customer_support.escalation_and_incident.major_incident_communication, and confusing the two produces a review written while people are still fixing things.

| State | Means | Entered when | Implies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `draft` | Timeline being assembled. The highest-value state and the shortest-lived. Everything gathered here from artefacts is checkable; everything gathered after the review meeting is recollection wearing a timestamp.  | — |  |
| `submitted` | Circulated for contribution before the room meets. Skipping this state is what produces a review where one person narrates and four people nod. | — |  |
| `pending_approval` | Under blameless review, meaning someone is reading it for attribution and for whether the detection and communication sections exist at all — not for whether the engineering is right. Those are different reads and collapsing them means only the second happens.  | — |  |
| `published` | The internal version is out. Deliberately NOT terminal. Treating publication as the end is the failure this whole object is arranged around, and a lifecycle that ends here would encode exactly that mistake into the software.  | — | The learning is recorded. Nothing has changed yet. |
| `in_progress` | Actions owned and being worked. The only state in which the postmortem is doing what it exists to do. | — |  |
| `overdue` | At least one action is past its date with nothing sent. A state rather than a flag, because what happens next differs — chasing an overdue postmortem action is a different motion with a different owner from writing one, and organisations that model it as an attribute discover their action debt at the annual review.  | `days_since(commitment.due_at) >= 7` AND `no_obs: followup_sent` |  |
| `closed` | Every action completed with evidence, or consciously abandoned with a stated reason. Both are legitimate closings and the second is far better than silence. | — |  |
| `superseded` | A recurrence produced a newer review of the same failure mode. Carries the previous incomplete action list forward rather than restating it — see the exception on recurrence, which argues this state should usually be reached by reopening rather than by reissuing.  | — |  |
| `archived` | Kept for the record. Findable, cited, and no longer tracked. | — |  |


## Inference patterns — 9 executable, 9 blocked


### Executable against the pipeline today

| Pattern | Kind | Reads | Yields | Statement | False positive |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `postmortem.action_overdue_with_no_outbound` | deterministic | `days_since(commitment.due_at) >= 7` AND `no_obs: followup_sent` | 7800 bp → `action_status` | An action from this review is at least a week past its date and no follow-up has been observed — the action list is decaying. | The action was completed in a system the pipeline cannot see. Postmortem actions land in Jira, Linear and GitHub far more often than in email, so a shipped fix and an abandoned one produce an identical trace here. This is the dominant false positive on this pattern and it is not rare — it is the normal case at any engineering-led organisation.  |
| `postmortem.action_carries_no_date` | deterministic | `exists: commitment.action` AND `absent: commitment.due_at` | 6800 bp → `actions_with_date_count` | An action was recorded with no due date at all — this is the diary-entry shape, and it is visible in the substrate today. | The date was stated in a form the extractor could not resolve — "by end of quarter", "before the next release", "when the migration lands". Those are genuinely worse than a date and genuinely not absent, so the pattern is right about the substance and wrong about the mechanism, which will make it look broken to whoever reviews the evidence.  |
| `postmortem.review_held_but_nothing_circulated` | deterministic | `days_since(meeting.start_at) >= 3` AND `no_obs: followup_sent` | 6500 bp → `action_status` | The review meeting happened at least three days ago and nothing has gone out in writing since. | The document was written straight into a wiki and never emailed, which is the standard workflow at most companies. A recurring incident-review standing meeting attached to the same graph node will also fire this every week forever.  |
| `postmortem.audience_turned_contractual` | heuristic | `has_obs: legal_review` | 6400 bp → `is_customer_facing` | Legal review has appeared on this thread — the postmortem has stopped being a learning artefact and become a commercial one. | `legal_review` fires on ordinary contract redlines happening in parallel on the same account — a renewal being papered in the same fortnight as an outage is common and entirely unrelated. The observation kind was built for a sales motion and carries no notion of what the review is about.  |
| `postmortem.feeding_a_customer_security_review` | heuristic | `has_obs: security_review_started` | 6000 bp → `audience` | The customer has opened a security review on the back of this incident, so the postmortem is now an input to their assessment of us. | A scheduled annual vendor security review landing in the same window as an incident. The coincidence is common at enterprise accounts, where reviews are calendar-driven, and this pattern cannot tell a triggered review from a routine one.  |
| `postmortem.actions_keep_slipping` | heuristic | `exists: commitment.action` AND `has_obs: timeline_slip` | 5800 bp → `action_status` | The action list has been re-dated — an action exists and a timeline slip has been observed on the same thread. | On a postmortem thread the word "timeline" is everywhere — it is the name of the document's best section — so `timeline_slip` is noisier here than on any other node in the domain. An extractor reading "the timeline slipped by forty minutes before anyone noticed", which is a statement about the INCIDENT, will fire this pattern about the ACTIONS.  |
| `postmortem.went_quiet_with_actions_open` | heuristic | `derived.engagement <= 0.5` AND `exists: commitment.action` | 5000 bp → `action_status` | Two-way discussion has halved while actions are still on the list — everyone has moved on. | The healthy case looks identical. This pattern cannot distinguish "abandoned" from "delegated properly", and those want opposite responses.  |
| `postmortem.landed_badly_with_the_reader` | heuristic | `derived.sentiment < 0.0` AND `thread.ball_in_court = us` | 4800 bp → `reader_sentiment` | Sentiment has turned negative on the review thread while the ball is in our court — the document did not do its job. | A postmortem thread is full of negative language by construction — it is a discussion of a failure, and an honest one uses words like "broken", "missed" and "failed" throughout. This pattern will read a rigorous, well-received review as a badly received one, and it will do so consistently rather than occasionally.  |
| `postmortem.written_by_almost_nobody` | heuristic | `edge_count <= 2` | 3800 bp → `contributor_count` | Very few people are attached to this review — the timeline is one person's account. | A sparse graph makes every node low-degree, so on a thinly-ingested tenant this fires on every postmortem including the well-attended ones. It also fires correctly-but-uselessly on the small incident that a single person reviewed in ten minutes, which the first exception argues is the RIGHT outcome.  |


### Blocked — needs a signal the pipeline does not emit

| Pattern | Kind | Needs | Would yield | Statement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `postmortem.exists_and_was_reviewed` | deterministic | `incident_declared` (obs_kind), `incident.status` (fact_path), `incident_resolved` (obs_kind) | 10000 bp | A postmortem exists for this incident, with a recorded review and a published document. |
| `postmortem.detection_gap_is_the_headline` | deterministic | `incident.started_at` (fact_path), `incident.detected_at` (fact_path), `ticket.created_at` (fact_path) | 9500 bp | The time between the system breaking and anyone inside the company knowing, stated as a number and tracked across reviews. |
| `postmortem.owed_by_severity` | deterministic | `incident.severity` (fact_path), `incident_resolved` (obs_kind), `incident.started_at` (fact_path) | 9000 bp | This incident's severity obliges a postmortem, and none exists. |
| `postmortem.this_has_been_written_before` | deterministic | `root_cause_identified` (obs_kind), `incident.severity` (fact_path), `derived.escalation_pressure` (derived) | 9200 bp | A prior postmortem already names this root cause, and its actions were not completed. |
| `postmortem.actions_never_reached_engineering` | deterministic | `bug_filed` (obs_kind), `handoff_to_engineering` (obs_kind), `bug_fixed` (obs_kind) | 8500 bp | The review produced actions, and none of them became a tracked engineering artefact. |
| `postmortem.blame_language_in_the_timeline` | heuristic | `blame_attribution` (obs_kind), `angry_language` (obs_kind) | 8000 bp | A named individual appears in the timeline where a role would have done. |

| `postmortem.timeline_is_recollection` | heuristic | `ticket.created_at` (fact_path), `incident_declared` (obs_kind), `first_response_time` (baseline) | 7000 bp | The timeline was assembled from memory rather than from artefacts, so every duration in it is an estimate. |
| `postmortem.customer_rca_owed_and_late` | heuristic | `entitlement.plan` (fact_path), `rca_requested` (obs_kind), `entitlement.expires_at` (fact_path) | 8800 bp | A customer is contractually owed a written RCA and the clock on it has passed. |

| Factor | Weight | Direction | Reads |

## Preconditions

- **`postmortem.impact_must_have_stopped`** A postmortem may not be started while customer impact is ongoing. _(unmet → block)_
- **`postmortem.timeline_before_the_room`** An artefact-backed timeline must be assembled before anyone is asked what happened. _(unmet → degrade)_
- **`postmortem.facilitator_was_not_the_responder`** The person facilitating should not have been on the response. _(unmet → degrade)_
- **`postmortem.blameless_contract_stated`** The blameless contract must be stated out loud at the start of the review, not assumed from culture. _(unmet → degrade)_
- **`postmortem.recurrence_checked_first`** Whether this failure mode has been reviewed before must be established before a new document is opened. _(unmet → block)_


## Constraints

- **`postmortem.exactly_one_incident`** A postmortem documents exactly one incident.
- **`postmortem.action_requires_owner_and_date`** An entry with no named person and no date may not be recorded as an action.
- **`postmortem.no_individual_named_in_the_timeline`** The timeline names roles, never individuals.
- **`postmortem.internal_and_external_are_separate_documents`** The internal and customer-facing versions are separate artefacts and may not be the same document with sections hidden.
- **`postmortem.detection_gap_must_be_stated`** The detection gap must appear as a number, including when it is zero. _(soft)_
- **`postmortem.root_cause_may_be_unknown_but_not_blank`** A stated unknown is an acceptable root cause. A blank field is not. _(soft)_
- **`postmortem.recurrence_reopens_rather_than_reissues`** A recurrence should reopen the prior review rather than open a new one. _(soft)_


## Business rules

- **`postmortem.ownerless_actions_are_not_actions`** An action without a named individual and a date is not an action. A team is not an owner — "Platform will add alerting" has the grammatical form of an action and none of the properties of one, because no individual wakes up owning it.
 — _This is the single most common way a well-attended, well-written review produces nothing, and it is invisible at the moment it happens because the list looks full._
- **`postmortem.action_needs_a_date`** An action recorded with no due date must be rejected at authoring time rather than discovered at the next review. — _Executable today against the commitment substrate, which makes this the one rule on this object that can be enforced at the moment of writing rather than argued about a quarter later._
- **`postmortem.overdue_action_is_a_finding`** An action a week past its date with nothing sent is a finding about the organisation, not an administrative oversight. — _The useful question is never "why is this late". It is "what outranked it", and the answer is almost never "nothing" — which makes it a prioritisation finding worth more than the action._
- **`postmortem.blameless_by_construction`** The timeline names roles and affordances, never individuals, and the blameless contract is stated aloud rather than assumed. — _Blamelessness is not a courtesy extended to the person who pushed the button. It is the only mechanism that produces a true timeline, because people who expect consequences report a defensible version rather than an accurate one — usually without noticing they are doing it._
- **`postmortem.two_audiences_two_documents`** A postmortem written for customers and one written for engineers are different documents and must be authored separately from one shared timeline. — _Merging them produces one that serves neither. In practice the internal version gets sanitised until it stops being useful for learning, which is the failure nobody notices because the document still exists and still gets praised._
- **`postmortem.detection_before_cause`** The detection timeline is written before the causal narrative. — _Whoever writes the cause first anchors the entire review on it, and the detection gap then gets described relative to a story that already has an ending._
- **`postmortem.recurrence_reopens_the_original`** When the same failure mode recurs, reopen the prior postmortem with its incomplete actions rather than opening a new one. — _A second document lets the organisation feel productive about the same failure twice, and it makes the recurrence count invisible by spreading it across two action lists._
- **`postmortem.single_root_cause_is_a_smell`** A review claiming exactly one root cause should be challenged before publication. — _Complex systems fail through combinations. Naming one cause usually names the last thing that changed and leaves the other conditions live — one of them produces the next incident, and it will look unrelated._
- **`postmortem.severity_downgrade_must_be_recorded`** A severity reassessed downward at review is recorded on the postmortem and does not retroactively alter the incident record. — _Quietly restating severity after the fact is how a team's declared-sev1 count falls without its outage minutes changing, and it corrupts the one field incident analysis depends on._
- **`postmortem.publication_is_not_completion`** A postmortem may not be marked complete at publication. It completes when its actions complete or are consciously abandoned with a reason. — _Treating publication as the end is the failure this whole object is arranged around, and a lifecycle that permitted it would encode the mistake into the software._


## Exceptions — where the rules above are legitimately wrong

- **An incident whose blast radius, duration AND detection gap are all small does not earn a postmortem. The correct output is one line on the issue and nothing else.
** — The process has a fixed human cost — a facilitated hour plus four or five people plus the write-up — and spending it on a nine-minute degradation with a two-minute detection gap trains everyone in the room to treat the ritual as paperwork. That training is the actual damage: it is spent from the same budget as the review that mattered, and it is spent first. The important qualifier is the AND, and it is the half teams get wrong: severity is not the only trigger. A four-minute outage that took six hours to notice earns a full review at any severity, because the detection gap is the finding and it is entirely severity-independent. Declining a review is a decision and must be recorded as one — see postmortem.decline_a_review — because a declined review with a stated reason is auditable and an omission is not.
 _(overrides postmortem.owed_by_severity, postmortem.recurrence_checked_first, postmortem.exactly_one_incident)_
- **When the same failure mode recurs and a prior postmortem exists, the correct output is NOT a new postmortem. It is the previous one, reopened, with its incomplete actions, the names of who owned them, and a written answer to what displaced them.
** — Writing a second document is how an organisation feels productive about the same failure twice. The costs are concrete rather than aesthetic: two half-done action lists now exist and neither is authoritative; the recurrence count is invisible because it is spread across two documents; and the second review will independently rediscover the first review's findings, which feels like rigour and is repetition. The genuinely useful output of a recurrence is not causal at all — the technical cause is already written down and was already correct. It is the answer to "what outranked the action", and that answer is almost never "nothing". It is usually a named piece of roadmap work, and naming it is the only version of this review that changes anything.
 _(overrides postmortem.this_has_been_written_before, postmortem.recurrence_reopens_the_original, postmortem.owed_by_severity)_
- **When the contributing condition was a consciously accepted trade-off rather than a miss, the action is to re-price the risk with the people who accepted it — not to fix the code.
** — A review that treats an accepted risk as an oversight produces an action nobody will do, because the person who would do it already decided not to and their reasons have not changed. The honest output is a decision record addressed to whoever owns the trade-off, which will frequently have no engineering owner and no date in the usual sense — which is why this exception has to suspend the ownership rule rather than work around it.
 _(overrides postmortem.single_root_cause_is_a_smell, postmortem.ownerless_actions_are_not_actions)_
- **Where counsel, a regulator or a discoverable-document regime is involved, the organisation cannot promise that the internal account will stay internal, and must say so before the review rather than after it.
** — Blamelessness is a promise about consequences. Under legal hold the organisation is no longer the only party deciding what the consequences are, and pretending otherwise is worse than dropping the promise — people who later discover the account was discoverable stop participating in every future review, not just this one. The correct move is to say it up front, run the review knowing it, and accept a thinner timeline as the price. That is a real loss and it should be recorded as one.
 _(overrides postmortem.blameless_by_construction, postmortem.internal_and_external_are_separate_documents)_
- **A security incident's review runs under a different owner, different distribution and legal involvement. It is not a support postmortem with extra care.
** — Running it as a support postmortem leaks — the distribution list is wrong by default, the timeline contains attack detail, and the customer-facing version has disclosure obligations with statutory clocks that have nothing to do with this object's conventions. The correct behaviour here is to hand off and to know that you have, which is why this exception exists as an explicit boundary rather than as a caveat inside the normal process.
 _(overrides postmortem.two_audiences_two_documents, postmortem.exactly_one_incident)_


## Best practices

- **Assemble the detection timeline from artefacts before anyone is asked what happened, and write it before the causal narrative.** — Whoever writes the cause first anchors the whole review on it, and the detection gap then gets described relative to a story that already has an ending.
- **Have the review facilitated by someone who was not on the response.** — A facilitator who was up all night fixing it cannot ask "why did that seem like the right call at the time" without the room hearing an accusation, however they phrase it.
- **Every action carries an individual's name and a date, or it moves to "things we noticed" and is labelled as such.** — The honest label is worth more than the false one. A list of six actions of which two are real is worse than a list of two, because nobody knows which two.
- **Ask what would have made this materially worse, and whether we avoided it by design or by accident.** — The closest thing to a free finding in the genre. It names the next incident before it happens, and it is the question most reliably left out because it feels speculative.
- **Have support write the detection and communication sections, not engineering.** — Support usually knows first, holds the arrival timestamps, and is the only function that experienced the comms failure directly. Engineering-owned reviews reliably produce a superb fix section and a one-sentence detection section.
- **Track postmortem actions in the same system as ordinary engineering work, never in the document.** — Actions tracked in a document compete with a backlog they are not in, and lose silently every time.
- **Count recurrences on the postmortem rather than on the incident.** — Incidents are genuinely distinct events and each looks new. The thing that repeats is the failure mode, and this document is the only place it has a name.
- **State the detection gap as a number in every review, including when it is zero.** — A number that is only reported when it is bad cannot be trended, and an untrended gap is indistinguishable from one that is not improving.


## Anti-patterns

- **The action item that reads "add more monitoring" with no named signal, threshold, destination or owner.** — tempting because It is true, it is uncontroversial, everyone in the room agrees with it immediately, and it costs nothing to write. It also sounds like exactly the right lesson from an incident that took too long to detect, which is what makes it so hard to object to in the moment.
 Instead: Name the signal, the threshold, where the alert goes, and who will be paged by it. If none of those can be answered in the room, the action is "decide what would have caught this", owned by a person, dated.
- **Merging the customer version and the engineering version into a single document.** — tempting because Writing two documents feels like duplicated work, the engineering one is already written, and the customer deadline is the one with a contract behind it. Nobody decides to merge them; the external deadline simply arrives first and the internal document is what exists.
 Instead: One shared timeline, two documents. The customer one says impact, cause in a sentence, and what changes by when. The internal one says everything, including the wrong guesses.
- **Treating the published document as the completion of the work.** — tempting because The document is the visible artefact, the meeting has a scheduled end, and everyone involved genuinely did produce something good. There is no moment at which anyone decides to stop. Instead: The lifecycle continues past `published` into `in_progress` and `overdue`, and closure requires either evidence of completion or a conscious abandonment with a stated reason.
- **Naming a specific person in the timeline where a role would have served.** — tempting because It is the most precise way to describe what happened, and precision reads as rigour. In a team that trusts each other it also feels harmless — the person is in the room, nobody is angry, and softening it feels like euphemism.
 Instead: Name the role and the affordance — what made it possible for that action to have that effect. "The deploy tool allowed a single confirmation to reach all regions" is both more precise and more actionable than any sentence containing a name.
- **Declaring exactly one root cause.** — tempting because Reviewers want a satisfying answer, a single cause is much easier to write an action against, and the format of most templates has one field. Instead: List contributing conditions, each of which had to be true. Then ask which single one, removed, would have prevented it — and notice how often the answer is "none of them alone".
- **Reviewing what broke and how it was fixed, while skipping detection and customer communication entirely.** — tempting because Engineering owns the review, the fix is the engineering-shaped part, and it is the part where everyone in the room has expertise. The detection gap belongs to nobody and the comms failure belongs to whoever was answering tickets at 3am, who is usually not invited.
 Instead: Support writes the detection and communication sections. Detection is written first and the gap is stated as a number.

- **email** — last message on the review thread

## Outputs

- **`detection_gap_minutes`** Time from breaking to knowing. The number this object exists to produce and the one worth trending across every review in a year. → L4.reasoning_unit, L6.learning_unit
- **`action_debt`** Open actions past their date across all postmortems. The organisation's real learning balance sheet, and a number almost nobody computes because it is embarrassing. → L4.decision_maker, L6.learning_unit
- **`recurrence_flag`** Whether this failure mode has been reviewed before. Changes the correct output from "write one" to "reopen the last one". → L4.decision_maker, L4.reasoning_unit
- **`customer_rca_owed`** Whether a written external RCA is contractually due, and to whom. → L5.communication_planning, L5.2.channel_planner
- **`learning_confidence_bp`** How much of this document should be believed, given timeline provenance and contributor breadth. A recollection-sourced timeline with one contributor should not feed a systemic conclusion at full weight. → L6.learning_unit
- **`systemic_theme`** The pattern across postmortems that no single one contains. The only output here that requires more than one instance of this object to exist. → L6.learning_unit
- **`credit_exposure_signal`** Whether this review is likely to be read as evidence in a service-credit or renewal conversation. Changes who writes it and what may be in it. → L4.reasoning_unit, L4.decision_maker


## Events

- **`postmortem.opened`** Postmortem Opened
- **`postmortem.timeline_assembled`** Timeline Assembled From Artefacts
- **`postmortem.review_held`** Blameless Review Held
- **`postmortem.published`** Postmortem Published
- **`postmortem.action_overdue`** Postmortem Action Overdue
- **`postmortem.customer_rca_sent`** Customer RCA Sent
- **`postmortem.recurrence_detected`** Recurrence Detected — invalidates action_status, prior_actions_completed, examines_detection
- **`postmortem.actions_closed`** All Actions Closed
- **`postmortem.superseded`** Superseded By A Later Review


## Actions

- **Build the timeline from logs, pages and ticket arrivals** (system) — Produces a checkable timeline before anyone is asked what they remember. The single highest-leverage step and the one most often skipped because the meeting is already scheduled.
- **State the blameless contract aloud** (human) — Makes the promise explicit and therefore breakable. A team that has never said it out loud has not made it and cannot be held to it.
- **Facilitate with someone who was not on the response** (human) — Lets the question "why did that seem right at the time" be asked without the room hearing an accusation.
- **Put a person and a date on every action** (human) — Converts the list from a record of a conversation into a plan. Anything that cannot take a name and a date moves to "things we noticed", honestly labelled.
- **File the actions where engineering actually works** (system) — The best available predictor of completion. An action existing only in this document has not left the room, whatever its owner and date say.
- **Write the external document separately from the internal one** (human) — One shared timeline, two documents, two audiences. Prevents the sanitisation that quietly destroys the internal version's usefulness.
- **Send the customer RCA** (agent) — Satisfies the contractual deadline and closes the incident for the account. Says what changes and by when; does not narrate the debugging.
- **Chase an overdue action and record what displaced it** (agent) — Recovers the action or produces the better finding. "What outranked it" is a prioritisation answer and it is worth more than the action was.

- **Reopen the previous review instead of writing a new one** (human) — Keeps one authoritative action list and makes the recurrence count visible. The move almost no process supports and the correct one on any repeat.
- **Record a decision NOT to review, with the reason** (human) — Makes the exception legible. A team that reviews everything reviews nothing seriously; a declined review with a stated reason is a governance artefact, and an undeclared one is an omission nobody can audit.

- **Close each action against evidence, or abandon it with a reason** (human) — Both endings are legitimate. Ticking a box before a meeting is neither.


## Evidence

- **telemetry** · 9500 bp — When it actually started and stopped, independent of anyone's account. The only source that can contradict every human in the room and be right, and therefore the only one that can establish a detection gap nobody can argue with.

- **slack** · 9000 bp — The incident channel. Timestamped, unrehearsed, and written by people who did not yet know how the story ended — which is exactly what makes it better evidence than the same people's recollection a week later. The single best artefact for this object and not ingested.

- **ticket** · 8500 bp — Arrival timestamps of the cluster. Frequently earlier than the first alert, and the cheapest honest proxy for started_at available to anyone.
- **status_page** · 8000 bp — The timeline as customers saw it and the only version they can check ours against. Proves what we said and when, which is the comms half of the review.
- **email** · 7000 bp — The review thread and the action list as written. Strong on commitments, weak on the timeline, and the only source the pipeline actually has today.
- **calendar** · 5500 bp — Proves a review was scheduled. Does not prove it happened, that anyone contributed, or that a document exists.
- **document** · 5000 bp — The postmortem itself. Deliberately mid-table rather than top: this object's discriminator is that the document is a CLAIM, so it is evidence of what was concluded and not of what occurred. Decays because a published postmortem is frozen while the system it describes keeps changing.

- **manual_entry** · 3000 bp — What people remember, written down. Honest, unverifiable, and decaying faster than anyone assumes — memory of an incident degrades faster than memory of almost anything else people do at work.


## Metrics

- **time_to_detect** (minutes) — Breaking to knowing. The number this object exists to move, and the one almost nobody trends.
- **time_to_declare** (minutes) — Knowing to declaring. Measures culture rather than tooling — if it is large, ask who felt they needed permission.
- **postmortem_completion_lag** (days) — Incident resolution to published document. Beyond about a week the timeline is recollection regardless of what the document claims.
- **action_ownership_rate** (percent) — Share of actions carrying a named individual AND a date. The diary-entry ratio.
- **action_completion_rate** (percent) — Share of actions completed with evidence rather than asserted. The only metric here that describes whether the practice works.
- **recurrence_rate** (percent) — Share of incidents whose failure mode had already been reviewed. Rises quietly and is the strongest available indictment of an action-tracking process.
- **detection_gap_trend** (minutes) — The gap across reviews over time. The single number that says whether any of this produced anything, and the reason detection deserves its own metric rather than a sentence.
- **customer_rca_turnaround** (days) — Request to delivery of the external document. The only deadline on this object anyone outside the company can enforce, which is why it wins by default.
- **blameless_language_violations** (count) — Individuals named in timelines. A count of zero proves nothing on its own; a count that rises predicts a fall in contributor_count two reviews later.

## Examples

- **Four-minute outage, six-hour detection gap** _(edge)_ — The incident nobody would review on severity and the one with the most valuable finding in the quarter. Impact was trivial; the fact that the same fault could have run for six hours before anyone noticed is not. This is the case the first exception's AND clause exists to protect.

- **An incident record that is right and a postmortem that is wrong** _(misclassification)_ — The incident says impact ran 47 minutes. The postmortem says 12, because whoever wrote it started the timeline at declaration instead of onset. Both documents are internally consistent, the postmortem is more widely read, and the detection gap has been deleted from the exact document that exists to find it. The discriminator, made concrete.

- **The same database failover, third time in fourteen months** _(edge)_ — Three incidents, three postmortems, three action lists, none complete. Each review independently rediscovered the same cause and felt rigorous doing it. The only useful output available on the third occasion was the answer to what outranked the actions the first two times, and no template had a field for it.

- **Published, praised, and nothing shipped** _(typical)_ — The modal outcome. Attended by nine people, quoted in an all-hands, six actions with team names and no dates. Nobody did anything wrong at any single moment.
- **One document sent to the customer and to engineering** _(misclassification)_ — Written to the customer deadline because that was the one with a contract behind it. Contains no wrong guesses, no component names and no honest account of the debugging — so it is unobjectionable and completely useless as a learning artefact, and it is the version now stored as the postmortem of record.

- **The on-call engineer named in the timeline** _(counterexample)_ — "At 02:14 Sam restarted the wrong node." Precise, true, and the last unprompted detail Sam's team volunteered for a year. The cost was invisible at the moment it was typed and was paid by four subsequent reviews.

- **Sev1 declared, sev3 at review** _(edge)_ — A correct downgrade with hindsight, and the finding is that declaring was cheap and right. Recorded on the postmortem rather than applied back to the incident — quietly restating it is how a declared-sev1 count falls without outage minutes changing.

- **An accepted risk that fired** _(edge)_ — The single-region failover was a documented trade-off made eighteen months earlier with the cost written down. Treating it as an oversight produces an action the accepting party already declined. The honest output is a decision record addressed to them, which no postmortem template has room for.

- **Four hundred tickets, no postmortem** _(misclassification)_ — Resolved in eleven minutes, so it cleared the severity bar for a review by duration and missed it by impact. Four hundred customers experienced it and the detection came from ticket volume — which is the finding, and it was never written down.


## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional** · completeness **complete**


> Scoped object, and the file says why in three places rather than one: the header comment, the identity block's owner_capability, and the owning capability.yaml's note. It is a document about ONE incident, produced by ONE capability, and nothing in triage or the queue reads it — what they need from a past incident is an issue and a root_cause, both core, both PRODUCED by this object. A second capability asking to load this is a symptom, not a promotion.
NINE patterns are executable today and NINE are not. That ratio is unusually good for this domain and it is an accident of vocabulary rather than a sign that postmortems are well instrumented: a postmortem action item is structurally identical to "I'll get back to you Thursday", so commitment.action, commitment.due_at and no_obs:followup_sent read an action list without modification. The two best executable patterns fall straight out of that — the overdue action with nothing sent, and the action recorded with no date at all, which is the diary-entry test expressed in the substrate. Three more read commercial observation kinds that genuinely fire on post-incident threads (legal_review, security_review_started, timeline_slip), and the last three read meeting timing, engagement collapse and graph degree, and are honestly scored at 3800-5000 because each has a false positive that fires as often as the true case. Every executable pattern here carries a `false_positive`, and three of them describe a case that is at least as common as the finding.
NOT ONE executable pattern touches the detection timeline, which is the section this object argues is the most valuable in the document. postmortem.detection_gap_is_the_headline is the top-ranked needs_signal and it needs a PAIR — incident.started_at and incident.detected_at. Only the first is in planned_substrate today; shipping it alone would produce a dashboard that looks like incident analytics and cannot answer the single question this object exists to ask. Two names are asked for that are in no planned list at all and should be: obs_kind blame_attribution (individuals named in a timeline, cheap to detect, and its absence is why blamelessness erodes without anyone deciding to abandon it) and obs_kind rca_requested (stated in plain language on threads already ingested, and the moment the postmortem acquires a second audience).
The two exceptions the domain asked for are both here and both carry the argument rather than the rule: the incident too small to earn a review — with the AND clause that a small incident with a large detection gap earns one anyway — and the recurrence, where the correct output is not a second document but the first one reopened with a written answer to what displaced its actions. Three more exceptions cover the accepted risk that fired, blamelessness under legal hold, and the security incident that is a different process entirely.
decision_factors sum to exactly 10000, ranked detection gap first against the industry habit of ranking resolution time first. Resolution time mostly measures how hard the problem was. Detection time measures choices we made, is the cheapest thing in the incident to change, and has no owner — which is the whole argument of this file in one line.
